newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US creates 316,000 new jobs in July.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US creates 316,000 new jobs in July.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department said the economy added 316,000 new jobs in July compared to a revised 228,000 jobs in June. The jobless rate stood at 4.8 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected non-farm payrolls of 193,000 and a jobless rate of 4.9 percent.
ANTHONY CHAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANC ONE INVESTMENT
ADVISORS: "It really tells us that the Federal Reserve cannot put the 'Going Out of Business' sign up yet, or the 'Gone Fishing' sign ...
"Employment growth is probably still coming in too strong for the Fed to tolerate," added Chan, who was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

NANCY KIMMELMAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, TECHNICAL DATA: "We have the unemployment rate at the low end of its range now, and the change in payroll growth at the high end of its range. I think the Fed is on edge, and the (Treasury) market as well."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "The government did it to us again.

"We've got two back-to-back large increases in government hiring now, but the private sector employment is a bit weaker than (the government sector.) We are not generating wage pressure. We suspect that the economy is moving into dangerous territory, but there is no evidence that this is creating much of a problem."

MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DONALDSON LUFKIN & JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: The gains in the service sector "are not an aberration. Nothing in the numbers indicates it is an aberration. Most of that gain is real.
"The labor market remains tight, but we are not seeing that filter through wages," Schaja added.
"Bonds liked the fact that wages were flat. They are dismissing the fact that there were gains in nonfarm payrolls."
HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP:
"At first blush, the reaction might be negative. The labor market is tight, lots of jobs are being created and it looks like the economy is picking up in July.

"But when you look more closely at manufacturing and construction jobs, it seems to indicate that industrial production was not that strong in July, housing was not that strong, and a lot of this looks like it was in the government sector.

"You could make the case for some pick-up in economic activity, so on balance, it's a modest negative. Even though there's tightness in the labor market, we're not seeing upward pressure on wages," Johnson added.
NICK PERNA, CHIEF ECONOMIST, FLEET FINANCIAL SERVICES:

"It's a mixed report in the sense that I think the markets are going to spend sometime today trying to figure out what it really means. But the two significant things are the unemployment rate went back down to its recent low of 4.8 percent and there was a very large increase in jobs ... Net-net, it's a strong employment report as far as I'm concerned. The concerns are going to be shifting to rapid economic growth again.
Perna added that he did not expect the Fed to "do anything on the basis of this report."

CARY LEAHEY, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, HIGH FREQUENCY ECONOMICS: "This is one of those reports where the strongest part is the headline number with the big increase in jobs. However, the (Treasury) market's going to be helped, or at least offset the adverse headline with two facts: (1) wages are unchanged in the month of July, and (2) the aggregate hours worked last month were down about five or six ticks.

"So overall, because of the drop in total hours worked, the report is an ok report for the market and finally, the market knows that regardless how low the unemployment rate gets or how strongly job growth is, the Fed's not going to tighten until spending turns around.
"So while this is an important report, it's less important than retail sales reports for the next couple of months," he concluded.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
